title: Parting Shot
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Stormy Morse lost two partners to gun suicide. She didn’t know that the second one, Lewis Tabler, had made the National Rifle Association the beneficiary of his retirement savings through its planned-giving program. In this feature, co-published with The New Yorker, Mike Spies describes what happens when the NRA, which has long denied a connection between access to guns and suicide rates, comes to collect:

Fisher, the NRA’s planned-giving director … e-mailed Applied Industrial, pointing out that Tabler had been dead for two months, and that “accounts with properly designated beneficiaries” are “generally available for distribution within 7–10 business days.” He went on, “We want to do whatever is needed to make this a smooth process.”

Meanwhile, multiple debt collectors had filed claims against Tabler’s estate, and the register of wills informed Stormy that she also owed an inheritance tax, since she was now the sole owner of the home.

As a favor, a neighbor of Stormy’s who was a lawyer spoke to the NRA’s assistant general counsel, Sarah Gervase, on her behalf. The neighbor raised the possibility that the organization might give up some of the money, according to Gervase, who recounted the exchange in an e-mail with Applied Industrial in early June. Gervase wrote that she “informed” Stormy’s neighbor that the “NRA is not willing to settle this.” Tabler’s cause of death did not seem to have any bearing on the organization’s position.

More picks about gun control

The Smallest Victims: Why Does America Keep Allowing Toddlers to Shoot Themselves?

Suzy Khimm | NBC News | June 28, 2024 | 3,994 words

“Nearly every day, a child unintentionally fires a gun and injures or kills someone. It’s one of the most preventable forms of gun violence—but that doesn’t mean it’s easy to solve.”

Amor Eterno

Skip Hollandsworth | Texas Monthly | May 8, 2023 | 7,580 words

“One year ago, before the school shooting in Uvalde, Kimberly Mata-Rubio had never been on a plane or given a public speech or scolded a U.S. senator right there in his office. A year in the life of a grieving mother.”

Every Day I Worry My Kids Will Be Killed at School

Meg Conley | Harper’s Bazaar | April 6, 2023 | 1,833 words

“’Will I be okay?’ my children ask me as the mass shootings in America continue. None of us like my answer.”

title: The Glorious Disorder of Michael Ondaatje’s Early Work
author: @NewYorker
content:
In an interview with the Times, earlier this year, Clint Bentley, the Oscar-nominated director and screenwriter of the film “Train Dreams,” was asked to name his “favorite book that no one else has heard of.” Bentley’s answer? Michael Ondaatje’s “The Collected Works of Billy the Kid,” from 1970. Bentley described the book, which combines prose, poetry, and photographs, as “hard to categorize.” He added that, despite its obscurity, he had eventually come across someone else who had read it.

I must be in the minority, because all my friends (each one of them, for good or ill, writers or visual artists) have read that book. We routinely talk about its boldness and inventiveness. But Ondaatje’s best-known work, the first of his that I read, the one that made him an international star, was the novel “The English Patient,” published in 1992. It won the Booker Prize that year, and the marvellous screen adaptation, by Anthony Minghella, won the Oscar for Best Picture in 1997.

I got my first job as an assistant professor around the time that “The English Patient” came out—in those years, for people of the “tinted persuasion” (the phrase is Salman Rushdie’s), it was easy to find an entry into English departments in the U.S. if you wanted to teach post-colonial literature. “The English Patient” was a gift to my curriculum. The novel allowed me to foreground the politics of otherness artfully. My students and I discussed its critique of narrow nationalism—the conviction, expressed by the explorer Almásy, that “we are deformed by nation-states.”

What makes this idea more powerful, and even poignant, is the appearance, in the book, of Kirpal Singh, an Indian combat engineer, or sapper, who goes by Kip. He is defusing bombs that the Germans have left behind in the Italian countryside, the immediate setting for the novel. In this drama of war between the imperial powers, Kip acts as a moral agent. He is devastated by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. When reminded that the English patient isn’t really English, Kip replies, “American, French, I don’t care. When you start bombing the brown races of the world, you’re an Englishman.” In other words, there is difference, and then there is difference.

There was another way that “The English Patient” was of help to me. I was still young when I read it, and falling in love. “The heart,” the novel taught me, “is an organ of fire.” Ondaatje’s language was piercingly lyrical; I was keenly attentive to its precision regarding what, in academic seminars, got called “the representation of desire.” Theory, much of it unintelligible, was enjoying its moment of dominance in literature classrooms; “The English Patient,” in contrast, was about bodies, at war and in love; it dealt with emotional conflict and striking sensual details. I carried in my head bits of the novel, such as the question that the English patient asks his fellow-explorer: “Madox, what is the name of that hollow at the base of a woman’s neck? At the front. Here. What is it, does it have an official name? That hollow about the size of an impress of your thumb?” (Late in the novel, the answer that I had been curious about arrived: the hollow was, in the world of the book, called the vascular sizood.) Kip and a Canadian nurse, Hana, fall in love in an abandoned Italian villa; they are “discovering that in lovemaking there can be a whole civilisation, a whole country ahead of them.” I was a new immigrant in love, and, reading such words, I imagined sexual love as a new country.

Born in Sri Lanka to parents of Tamil, Dutch, and Sinhalese ancestry, Ondaatje is alert to his mixed identity and, it can easily be argued, has made it a part of his literary output. As a young boy, he immigrated to England and then, in his late teens, moved to Quebec. Still later, he taught in London, Ontario, and then in Toronto. In the decades prior to the publication of “The English Patient,” he was involved in collaborative literary publishing in Ontario, as a participant in the work of the avant-garde Coach House Press, and in the editing and production of the literary magazine Brick. Long before I learned of him, his poetry and fiction had received some of Canada’s major literary prizes, such as the Governor General’s Award, which he won multiple times, for both poetry and fiction, including “The Collected Works of Billy the Kid.”

In the years after the success of “The English Patient,” I, like many others, began to read Ondaatje’s earlier work. I cannot recall exactly my first response to “The Collected Works of Billy the Kid.” Did I find it disorienting? Perhaps I did. It was different from “The English Patient,” although there were continuities, such as in the use of archival materials. In “The Collected Works,” the reader encounters period photographs and brief poems and vignettes shaped from found objects and history. The sentences here are often short, with flinty speech seemingly farmed from Westerns: gory bits mixed with a kind of native poetry, a ground-level mythology that makes rough music on the page. Here, for instance, is how the outlaw known as William H. Bonney, or Billy the Kid, describes the killing of a man named Gregory:

I’d shot him well and carefulmade it explode under his heartso it wouldnt last long andwas about to walk awaywhen this chicken paddles out to himand as he was falling hops on his neckdigs the beak into his throatstraightens legs and heavesa red and blue vein out.

For some archival photographs, the image itself was missing, but a description was included. There had been a portrait that may have depicted the real-life Billy, and it could have been used, but Ondaatje was advised by his poet friend bpNichol to leave the space blank. In an essay for Brick, Ondaatje described bpNichol’s telling him, “Keep the lines, but take out the photo—let the reader imagine him”—advice that immediately appealed to Ondaatje’s aesthetic. But all this I learned much later; when I first read the book, I had to imagine not just what Billy the Kid looked like but also the author’s motivations and choices.

The next book of Ondaatje’s that I read was his first novel, “Coming Through Slaughter,” from 1976. It tells the story of one of history’s legendary jazz players, Buddy Bolden, in New Orleans at the turn of the last century. Bolden works as a barber during the day, and as a cornet player at night. Here again, in this slim book, the narrative unfolds in fragments, every sentence drawing you deeper into the delights of language. I didn’t entirely grasp its movements, and I’m not embarrassed to admit that, despite my incomplete understanding, I put the book on the syllabus for a course on novellas. I wanted my students to get in touch with the book’s defiant incompleteness—and also its wholeness. It was important that they understood how lovely and improvisatory and unexpected everything was, page after page.

Academia teaches order. It wants conventional form; it rewards linearity (preferably accompanied by footnotes). In the first paragraph, you state what you are going to explore in the rest of the paper, and you repeat things when you reach your conclusion. Also, you are required to be consistent; you are not allowed to switch from prose to poetry to photographs. Even when I didn’t fully understand “Coming Through Slaughter,” I felt that Ondaatje could teach my students how to break the mold into which they thought all writing had to be poured. And, in teaching, I also wanted to teach myself to be audacious in my own writing. For me, the early challenge and lesson was always to try to grasp the poetic mystery of the collage form—the elusive instinct that guided Ondaatje to paste torn strips of narrative to make a surprising whole.

And then I read his memoir, “Running in the Family,” from 1982, the pages of which are peopled with characters of exquisite and eccentric charm. The book enacts, as if on a stage, the wild antics of Ondaatje’s alcoholic father, and his grandmother’s adventures during his childhood in Sri Lanka (“the island as we know it now, a pendant off the ear of India”). Its narrative takes the form of travel writing mixed with other reminiscences and interviews. There are old photographs, as if from a family album, and poems. It was in this book’s pages that I first read Ondaatje’s superb love poem “The Cinnamon Peeler,” which must rank as one of the most aromatic and ardent statements of sexual intent in the history of literature. (I’ve heard that this poem has been read at weddings, and has led, in at least one instance, to a grandmother fainting as she listened to the display of passion, a story that itself seems to have come right out of the pages of “Running in the Family.”) I began to see how each of Ondaatje’s books—poetic, expert, insouciant—pushed at and past the formal limits of expression.

And so, readerly understanding began to work in the other direction: the early work became the lens through which I understood later works, such as “The English Patient.” I had been drawn to that novel’s collision of origins and backgrounds (Ondaatje’s own word for this is “mongrelism”), but I came to value ever more the brilliance, the daring of its narrative structure, its risky use of gaps and mystery and silence.

Years later, I read a distillation of this principle in another book of Ondaatje’s, “The Conversations,” from 2002, a series of discussions with the film editor Walter Murch, who had won two Academy Awards for his work on “The English Patient.” In one passage, Ondaatje describes watching a film in which the cuts between scenes are done in such a way that each scene is “complete,” each one whole in itself. This, he writes, was dissatisfying. The reflections that follow reveal a near-mathematical formula through which Murch cuts a given scene—he holds back about one-fifth of the narrative, making a story that suddenly feels much more compelling because it requires our careful attention in order to be understood.

“The Conversations” clarified, for me, the fact that editing—the cutting of scenes—has been a, perhaps the, crucial part of Ondaatje’s writing. Cuts are even more visible in his poetry than in his fiction, more necessary to it. The whole business of poetry, the line breaks and stanzas, puts emphasis on imaginative edits and collaging. What Ondaatje went on to do was to smuggle such techniques into prose fiction, concealing them in plain sight, so that we move forward in our seats and listen more carefully.

Ondaatje’s interest in editing may also have roots in another facet of his career: the low-budget, experimental documentary films that he made in the nineteen-seventies. The most accomplished of these, “The Clinton Special” (1974), follows a group of actors from the Toronto-based Theatre Passe Muraille (Theatre Beyond Walls) who go into a rural Ontario community and produce a play based on what they see and hear from the people there. The actors are engaged in a difficult but heady experiment, and we get so caught up in watching them that we are liable to forget that Ondaatje is doing the same in his film.

A writer’s beginnings are obscure, and often banal. In “Running in the Family,” Ondaatje recalls his earliest encounters with writing. At St. Thomas’ College Boy School in Sri Lanka, he had been made to write lines, in Sinhala, as punishment for some schoolboy infraction or another. A hundred and fifty times: “We must not urinate again on Father Barnabus’ tires.” A hundred and fifty times: “I must not throw coconuts off the roof of Copplestone House.” Rote learning, repetitive writing, the curse of a colonial education. From those unpromising beginnings, Ondaatje found, in his writing, newness and, in language, a certain freedom. Later, for writers like me, who had crossed borders to arrive in the West and often made that crossing the subject of our work, Ondaatje’s example, particularly his disregard for the established boundaries through which genres were defined, taught us to spell out our own liberation in a similar fashion. It wasn’t enough to exchange one passport for another—to be a real writer you had to take risks and invent new forms. ♦

title: “The End of Oak Street” Is a Weirdly Alienated Jurassic Lark
author: @NewYorker
content:
The tough, steely competence of Anne Hathaway—the sense that her characters could shoulder the weight of the world, without complaint and on short notice—has been one of the more welcome recurring spectacles of this moviegoing year. No, she couldn’t save the recent “Mother Mary,” a tedious, logorrheic folly, in which she played a pop star in serious need of a new dress, some counselling, and a much better script. But she was unsurprisingly winning in “The Devil Wears Prada 2”: Hathaway made you believe that her character, caught up in the increasingly unsustainable realms of glossy journalism and high fashion, could engineer a fairy-tale solution to a real-world problem with masterly ease. Not that the actor’s expressive powers are limited to tales of the present; as the Ithacan queen Penelope in “The Odyssey,” she polished an ancient Greek vessel to a diamond-hard Hollywood lustre. The merits of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation have been much debated, but few could deny that, in a film of extreme narrative fragmentation, Hathaway’s genuinely regal presence insured that the emotional center held.

The new, strange, and junkily diverting suburban thriller “The End of Oak Street” provides a fascinating contrast in Hathaways and means. The actress stars as a Michigan wife, mother, and aspiring writer named Denise Platt, who, unlike Penelope, seems more than ready to end her marriage. Her recently laid-off husband, Greg (Ewan McGregor), is not sailing back from Troy—the year is 1982—but proves distant in every sense; he under-parents, over-drinks, and spends most of his time out of the house. At night, Denise retreats to the basement, not to unravel her weaving but to work on a novel that paints a none-too-flattering portrait of marriage and motherhood. (She and Greg have a teen-age daughter, Audrey, played by Maisy Stella, and a pre-teen son, Brian, played by Christian Convery.) After some laborious setup, the Platt household is under siege: instead of lecherous male suitors the threat is from dinosaurs, which, through some rift in the fabric of prehistory, are suddenly stomping and chomping their way through the neighborhood.

And Denise, rather than retreating from the action, unleashes a piercing battle cry and plunges into the mayhem head on. Not right away, of course. “The End of Oak Street” moves with agreeable briskness—it runs barely a hundred minutes—but the director and screenwriter, David Robert Mitchell, knows that even full-bore dinosaur high jinks need to be rationed and modulated. When all hell does eventually break loose, though, so does Denise: she fires a rifle at an Allosaurus, fends off pterosaurs with her bare hands, and, in the film’s thrilling highlight, stabs frenziedly with a kitchen knife at a slow-rolling, scene-stealing Titanoboa. (That’s scientific nomenclature for “giant-ass snake.”) Hathaway is no stranger to action movies, but seldom have her contributions to the form been so dirt-under-the-fingernails feral. Her versatility is remarkable. You believe her when, at the dinner table with Greg and the kids—before the neighborhood has gone all Cretaceous—a sad little smile lights up her face, as if she were already mourning the end of something precious. But you believe her even more when, seeing that same family threatened, she hurls herself into the fray without a second thought. It speaks to Hathaway’s abilities that, at any given moment, everything that Denise says, does, and feels makes crystalline sense, even when everyone and everything around her seems to do the opposite.

Mitchell springs his most inspired twist early on, and you should skip the rest of this paragraph if you care to experience it fresh. In short, it isn’t the dinosaurs that have come back; it’s Oak Street that has gone back. Inexplicable tremors, accompanied by haunting blips of white light, have ripped the neighborhood from its foundations and sent its homes and residents to the dawn of time, plunking them down on a landscape of smoking volcanoes, wildly overgrown jungle flora, and gargantuan theropods run amok. All this is figured out, with amusing if anticlimactic prescience, by Audrey, who’s blessed with a Carl Sagan-loving scientific mind. What she or anyone else is unable to determine is precisely why or how the space-time glitch occurred, and if Mitchell knows, he isn’t telling. He has, in his previous films, been happy to leave mysteries unsolved. In “It Follows” (2015), the specific origins of an unstoppable shape-shifting sex demon are left to the viewer’s imagination, and “Under the Silver Lake” (2019), a droll riff on L.A.-noir tropes, seemed to thumb its nose at the very idea of revelation or meaning. Such narrative caginess isn’t inherently a problem. The lack of a clear explanation for, say, the avian attacks in “The Birds” (1963) is crucial to its lasting unease and metaphorical power, and there are a few scenes here—as when Denise and Greg get trapped in a car, or when winged scavengers pick at the corpses of their freshly deceased neighbors—that function as direct homages to that Hitchcock classic.

“The End of Oak Street” is awash in such allusions. There are unmistakable flashes of Stephen King; a bully’s attack on Brian recalls the adolescent dynamics of “Stand by Me” (1986), and the vision of a neighborhood under siege, cut off from the rest of the world, evokes the supernatural entrapment of “Under the Dome.” Mostly, though, the film has been conceived as a fastidiously sun-drenched, nostalgia-rich homage to the early works of Steven Spielberg. It’s as if the raptors of “Jurassic Park” (1993) had inexplicably surfaced in the year of “E.T.” (1982), and you may flash back on that film as the sad spectre of divorce looms over the Platts, or when Brian and his buddies ride their bikes down Oak Street. The nocturnal disturbances in the neighborhood, all pulsing lights and ominous rumbles, hark back to the alien warning signs in “Close Encounters of the Third Kind” (1977). And, to an impressive degree, Mitchell has brought the underwater lessons of “Jaws” (1975) ashore, using the layouts of trees and houses to conceal his prehistoric predators from view. In one shot, the spikes of a stegosaurus’s tail, poking out over a row of foliage, wittily suggest a shark’s fin breaking the surface.

It’s possible that not even Spielberg himself, coming off this summer’s highly self-referential “Disclosure Day,” could have fashioned a more totalizing monument to his legacy. “The End of Oak Street” is far from the first wink-wink pastiche that his work has inspired, and in the best of them, the power of Spielberg’s iconography dovetails with, and is sufficiently transformed by, the younger filmmaker’s independent vision. That alchemy came close to happening in the case of the alien-invasion thriller “Super 8” (2011), whose director, J. J. Abrams, is a producer on Mitchell’s movie. (The two pictures also share a composer, Michael Giacchino, who, it’s worth noting, has also scored three entries in the “Jurassic World” franchise.) Far better was Jordan Peele’s U.F.O. thriller “Nope” (2022), which succeeded in not merely mimicking Spielberg’s conventions, but weaponizing them with an uncompromising darkness that, paradoxically, became both a grand example and a ferocious critique of Hollywood spectacle.

Mitchell’s own imitation of Spielbergian life, despite its meticulous re-creation (and gleeful destruction) of eighties suburbia, stumbles into an uncanny valley between sincerity and cynicism, between unintentional comedy and deliberate homage. It wouldn’t be inapt to say that the director knows the notes but not the music—but he has orchestrations of his own, and they produce distinctly fascinating dissonances. On a certain level, it’s hard to think of a filmmaker less temperamentally suited to channelling the wonderment and uplift of early Spielberg. Mitchell is, by nature, a poet of alienation, and his earlier films—including his wistful début feature, “The Myth of the American Sleepover” (2011)—have all been ruminations on the intense, often dangerous isolation of young people, even in the ostensibly supportive company of friends and lovers. In “Under the Silver Lake,” a young slacker vanishes down a conspiracy-theory rabbit hole; in “It Follows,” sex becomes a defensive weapon, wielded in a callous spirit of every person for themself.

It’s no surprise, then, that in “The End of Oak Street,” the Platts often seem terribly alone, boxed in, and disconnected from one another, though not, with the exception of Hathaway’s scenes, in ways that achieve a deeper poignancy or suggest a deliberate satire of suburban malaise. Throughout, Mitchell seems oddly incurious about his characters and the miniature sub-dramas he doles out to them, as if he were going through a set of dramaturgical motions that he doesn’t fully believe in. Greg is a schlumpy blank, and McGregor’s performance barely begins to fill him in. Brian is a gee-whiz irritant, with a reckless attachment to the family’s conveniently recalcitrant dog and a knack for making dangerous situations worse. Promisingly, Mitchell uses the trauma and tragedy of the dinosaur attacks to plant seeds of attraction between Audrey and another neighborhood girl, Jeannette (Jordan Alexa Davis), but the flowering of their feelings is observed from a weirdly detached remove—a perfunctory attempt to subvert the coming-of-age conventions of an earlier era.

It’s in the nature of Hollywood movies about cataclysmic disasters to invest our sympathies in a select few—a shaken family, a clutch of survivors—and to milk queasy, there-but-for-the-grace-of-God thrills from the death and suffering of the anonymous masses. That contrast needn’t feel like hypocrisy; in the hands of an assured filmmaker—say, the Spielberg of “War of the Worlds” (2005)—the seemingly arbitrary but utterly calculated nature of who lives and dies can leave us feeling more connected to humanity, rather than less. But Spielbergian humanism and Mitchellesque alienation are an oil-and-water combo, and the upshot, even within the context of a big-budget piece of summer escapism, is a nagging callousness—an indifference to the world beyond the film’s immediate dramatic purview. Again and again, the camera, wielded by the director of photography Mike Gioulakis, glides past scenes of horror and carnage with an elegance that verges on indifference. Various neighbors are programmatically sacrificed on the altar of the Platts’ survival and the audience’s presumed pleasure. It all builds to a feel-good final twist that, when you pause to consider its ramifications, is close to appalling in its sentimental self-absorption—a reminder that the dinosaurs, for whatever terror they instill, may not be the cruellest manifestations of their maker’s imagination. ♦

title: Why Millennial Professionals Are Embracing Socialism
author: @NewYorker
content:
During the past few weeks, I’ve heard from a lot of readers who have theories about Subaru Socialists, the term I used, in a recent column, to refer to middle-class, college-educated, liberal millennials. Some of the critics of this cohort blame colleges for pushing left-wing politics and engendering an excess of concern for struggling people; more sympathetic readers credit the work of community organizing and activism for generating those very same things. Reading these reactions has pushed me to consider a subset of the Subaru Socialists: professionals in their thirties and forties who are now basically doing fine financially, and may even belong to the upper middle class. It used to be a cliché that youthful idealism eventually gives way to fiscal conservatism (and to thinking way more than you ever expected you would about your taxes). How did this group veer away from that once seemingly inevitable trajectory?

A little self-reflection might be in order. Like many of my Subaru Socialist ilk, I went into debt for an arguably useless graduate degree—a Master of Fine Arts in fiction, from Columbia. After finishing that degree, I spent several years getting rejected by pretty much every publishing house and magazine there is. When the Great Recession happened, I was twenty-eight, and I lost my job as a private-school teacher, leading to an extended stay on unemployment. All of this felt bad, but I didn’t really channel it into the politics of the left until Bernie Sanders began showing up on campaign stages, in 2015. By then, I had paid off my student loans, had bought a home, and was making enough money as a writer that I no longer needed to feverishly check my account balances or worry too much about buying a plane ticket or new car parts.

As I have thought more about others like me—comfortable people in their forties who are nonetheless frustrated enough with capitalism and the Democratic establishment to vote for seemingly any insurgent candidate in sight—I’ve wondered why I started thinking seriously about universal health care, wealth redistribution, and the expansion of the public sector at the precise moment that I didn’t really need them anymore. An obvious answer would be that it’s hard to think very much about politics when you’re struggling to get your bank account consistently above five hundred dollars. But I find that unconvincing—even when things were bad, I wasn’t entirely immiserated, and I still read the news. I also can’t plead ignorance: I had a Marxist phase in college and spent my early twenties talking solemnly about revolutions and the proletariat. But those convictions were abstract, if sincere, and I suppose they stayed that way until Sanders came along.

What—or, rather, who—bridged my youthful communism and the softer populist politics of my thirties and forties? Barack Obama. I remember the excitement I felt after Obama’s victory in 2008 not as one recalls a moment in history that locks you into a time and a generation but more as something that happened to me, personally, like hitting a buzzer beater in a basketball game or going on a first date. Until the full reality of the financial crash and its aftermath set in, Obama and his great hope of multiethnic progress put my youthful questions about wealth inequality and the crimes of Wall Street at bay. I believed, as so many of us did, that we would all just float up to an era of prosperity and racial harmony. By the time Sanders came around, that vague hope had curdled into resentment. I wanted nothing to do with anti-racist, neoliberal corporate politics—during this time I took to stringing such terms together—even if I understood that they were probably good for me and my career, perhaps more so than tax policies that favored the upper middle class.

I should note that I do not think that Obama’s Presidency was a great failure; nor do I believe that Obama sold out the millions of acolytes who, upon seeing him take the stage at the Democratic National Convention in 2004 and deliver his “skinny kid with a funny name” speech, treated him like a saint. But his handling of the financial crash ultimately forced many of us to acknowledge that the floaty dream was over and that he had not delivered. An alternative was needed, one that felt bound both to a personality and to an idea. We didn’t know exactly who that alternative might be—even as Sanders gained momentum following his shocking win in the Michigan primary—but we knew, right away, who it was not: Hillary Clinton.

Subaru Socialism grew, in part, out of the 2008 crash, the subsequent disappointment in Obama, and a rejection of Clinton and her entitled, uninviting run at the Presidency. But why did it take the shape it did? Why the socialist bent? Couldn’t these same factors have led to a more centrist politics focussed on the repudiation of Donald Trump and on a celebration of free markets that could lift up new immigrants into a strong middle class?

There are multiple reasons. One is the cultural and political celebrity of Sanders. Also, our politics sometimes lags behind our economic reality. The first Sanders campaign made me realize that I did get kinda screwed on my student loans, and that things maybe shouldn’t have been so hard. I felt retrospective anger toward Columbia for offering a program that charged people fifty thousand dollars a year, guaranteed absolutely nothing in return, and seemed unconcerned with the debt that many of its students were piling up. Friends of mine from that program never recovered financially. I also came to appreciate the safety net provided by California’s unemployment benefits, which allowed me to figure out what I could do next—the 2008 crash didn’t doom me to eviction and starting over at my parents’ house (even if I eventually ended up there for a short time).

More than any of this, though, I felt inspired by Sanders’s universalist message, and by his refusal to participate in the factional, identity-based battles that I had long suspected served only as a kind of promotional package for the careers of politicians, academics, and corporate employees. This was part of the disappointment with Obama, too—the realization that even if more “people of color” moved up the corporate and political ladders, we would simply end up with a slightly more diverse ruling class.

Sometimes, politics takes root not at the point of misery, but years later, when the agita has passed and someone can explain why it had to be that way. It took me a few years to fully get on board with the left. The hope that Obama inspired in me died a bit more slowly than one might expect, in no small part because I am a minority and therefore especially attached to the idea of a prosperous, post-racial America. When I had children, though, I found myself moving further toward broad, fuzzy support for anything semi-socialist. My wife and I could afford child care, but we could also see just how little would have to change to make that impossible. And during the first Trump Presidency it became quite obvious to me that, although I had somehow become more successful as a writer than I ever could have imagined during my days of unemployment and rejection, the job was shakier and less stable than it would have been not that long before.

You could say the same about many jobs, particularly those in fields where you’re likely to find a lot of Subaru Socialists: academia, the arts, the entertainment industry, even advertising. All of these fields tend to require quite a bit of school and have far less stability than they once did. And people in these fields have done much to shape the thinking of their peers. Will Menaker, one of the hosts of the influential leftist podcast “Chapo Trap House,” is the son of Daniel Menaker, a longtime fiction editor at this magazine who later became the executive editor-in-chief of Random House. Will made a go of it in his father’s industry before becoming one of the most biting and incisive voices of the so-called Bernie Bro movement. His experience is particular and, as he freely admits, extremely privileged, but it’s also exemplary, to some degree. I listened to almost every episode of “Chapo Trap House” when it first launched, and I recall feeling both put off by Menaker’s culturally élite, private-school background and somewhat connected to him—because he and I were more or less seeing the same thing.

Menaker told me that he and his co-hosts did not set out to embody the anger of the downwardly mobile, middle-class youth, though it did ultimately shake out that way. This makes sense; no podcast or live stream—at least no very good one—started out with such an explicit political goal. But their show, like talk-radio shows of the past, provided a relatable, consistent voice that allowed listeners to see themselves a bit more clearly. One of the key dynamics of the Bernie Bro movement was that, although it talked about the working class, it also showed the previously privileged classes how to proletarianize themselves, in part by asking a simple question: If it sucks for us, how bad must it be for everyone else?

You could look at all this and conclude that Subaru Socialists such as myself are vain, unserious, and fully unsympathetic. After all, nobody made me go to an expensive graduate program—at Columbia, of all places—and it may even seem ungrateful to study at one of the most prestigious institutions on the planet and then get mad when it doesn’t yield what it seemed to promise (especially in my case, since it basically did). Nobody is entitled to work their dream job. But along with more personal disappointments came the realization that the industry I was hoping to enter might never get any healthier, and that this was true in those other fields as well, and many others besides. That forced me to think about my daughter and what protections she would need if, God forbid, she decided to try to become a writer like her father. Would she have health care? Could she ever afford to buy a home? How much wealth would be captured by the tech oligarchy, and how far would she be—despite growing up privileged by any standard—from earning some of that money? How close would she be to ending up in much worse shape than her parents?

Those are my politics of self-interest, and the reasons that the left keeps making sense to me, even as I burrow comfortably into the upper middle class. The children of the Subaru Socialists will almost certainly have it worse than their parents. No matter what sort of privileged and perhaps contradictory path you took to reach that conclusion, once you see it, you can’t look away. ♦

title: My pilgrimage to Mecca in the age of the golf-cart and mall | Aeon Essays
content:
It is Ramadan, the holiest month of the Islamic calendar, and I am sitting in a rooftop café in Mecca, the holiest city of the religion. The sun has gone down, and an array of glittering shops and hotels lights up the urban expanse below me. At the heart of this ancient city, the foremost site of Muslim worship, guarded with fortress-like marble walls, is the Masjid al-haram complex – the largest mosque in the world. I’ve just completed my own pilgrimage to the holy site, and I’m struggling to name the discomfort that I am feeling.

There are few words to describe the whiplash of coming face to face with a Joe & The Juice, a Sephora and a plethora of other shops and hotels and Times Square-style billboards after going through one of the most spiritually charged experiences of my life. To find myself in what seemed just like any other petrodollar-fuelled Gulf port instead of a sanctified land was jarring. I felt robbed of the romanticism I had expected after a childhood built on admiration for religious lore and high-flown notions of a fantastical divine city.

I’d found myself in Mecca, trying to catch a break from the existential dread of my day-to-day life – the constant round of applying for jobs I didn’t really want because it wasn’t sustainable to write full-time, going on first date after first date, trying to find love on apps that were designed for failure, doomscrolling social media while caught in a dopamine trap, and staring at my laptop screen while waiting for some revelation to break through the fog in my mind and string itself into life-changing words. My 30s were closing in, and I felt the noose of squandered potential around my neck.

One of my most frequent prayers comes from a verse in the Quran that narrates Moses’ escape from Egypt: ‘Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khairin faqir’ (‘My Lord, indeed I am in absolute need of whatever good You send down’). I have always been comforted by the notion that a divine power was looking after me, that something out there existed beyond the constraints of time and space – omnipresent, omnipotent – and yet closer to me than my jugular vein, as my Holy Book would tell me.

My rationale for the trip was that this kind of spiritual sugar rush would allow me to find my footing in the secular world. My worshipful hope was that God would be impressed by my performed devotion, and divine intervention would set my worldly affairs straight. And though I felt a sense of renewed worship in making my pilgrimage, that break from the ordinary world never came.

Islam is not an ascetic faith: interestingly, it prohibits monasticism. However, the state of being a pilgrim is the closest that one comes to forsaking the material world. Before entering the boundaries of the Holy City, dressed in a swishing white abaya with a prayer book hung on a lanyard around my neck, I had committed to a state of heightened spiritual purity known as the ihram.

The word ihram has etymological roots in the word haraam, which means to forbid. It is the embodiment of additional, out-of-the-ordinary prohibitions. In this consecrated state, pilgrims are not allowed to have sexual relations or to hunt an animal or to change the state of their body: they cannot cut their nails or hair, for example, or perfume themselves. Men must cover themselves only with two pieces of unstitched cloth, while women must wear unadorned garments that leave their faces and hands visible. The purpose of the ihram is to equalise worshippers for the duration of their pilgrimage. As the anthropologists Victor Turner and Edith Turner described (albeit in the context of Christianity), pilgrims occupy a liminal, threshold state. They enter a state of structural betweenness, termed ‘communitas’, where they find themselves stripped of their social identities, and in a temporary state of spontaneous egalitarianism.

There are two kinds of pilgrimages in the faith, the umrah – which takes a few hours to complete and can be done at any time of the year, and the Hajj – which takes five days, and can be performed only in the Islamic month of Dhul-Hijjah. Both pilgrimages require the same conditions of ihram. I began my umrah with a short ride to the Mosque on a government-funded shuttle service, decorated with an electric ticker that said: ‘Welcome Guests of Ar Rahman’, that is, guests of the Most Merciful. Pilgrims are not guests of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, but of God, and therefore, on paper, both prince and pauper must be alike. When in communitas, this sentiment feels enacted.

It is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you

Some pilgrims prayed on the shuttle with prayer beads, others read out verses from the Quran apps on their phones. Others still had prayer books similar to mine. But as we got closer to the Great Mosque, we were let off the bus, and everyone’s rhythmic chanting came into unison in a single phrase, as pilgrims cried out to the skies ‘Labbaik Allahumma Labbaik’ (‘Oh, here I am, my Lord! I have answered your call!’) The fervent declaration continued as we joined the crowd of thousands making their way on foot into the heart of Masjid al-Haram.

The first thing you experience when you enter the Great Mosque of Mecca is the smell of oudh and rosewater engulfing you. A cultural belief among many Muslim communities is that whatever you pray for when you first glance upon the Kaaba – the black raw-silk-covered cuboid stone at the centre of the mosque – will be granted, so most pilgrims enter for the first time with their eyes firmly planted on the cool marble floor – or held tightly shut as they hold on to the person guiding them in. And when you do open your eyes, that initial glance is surreal; an ocean of pilgrims clad in white circumambulate the Kaaba, flocks of swallows flit against the skyline, and there are hundreds of things in the periphery of your sightlines to be distracted by – from the towering malls to surveillance drones and battalions of guards with puffed chests patrolling against miscreants. Yet, despite these competing spectacles, it is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you – more enormous than you imagined, impossibly still, magnetic.

The Kaaba is an epitomic example of what Mircea Eliade, a foundational historian of religions, described in The Sacred and the Profane (1957) as ‘axis mundi’, or the navel of the Earth, a centre from which the world is said to have emerged. In Islamic belief, Mecca is the mother city, the land from which the rest of the world rolled out. In the same theology, the Kaaba was the first building on Earth, established for the worship of God, before being lost in the flood of Noah and then rebuilt by Abraham and his son Ismael in its present form.

Since Muhammad’s conquest of Mecca in 630 CE, the Kaaba has oriented all aspects of Muslim life. Wherever they are in the world, Muslims perform their five daily prayers facing towards the Kaaba, and dead bodies are buried with their head oriented in the same direction. The complex built around it encompasses all of the sacred topography you must go through on your pilgrimage. You start with the circumambulation of the Kaaba, before praying adjacent to the Maqam-e-Ibrahim, a stone enclosed in glass, which is supposed to bear the footprints of Abraham. Then, you must cross the distance between the hills of Safa and Marwa seven times, a total of 3.15 km (1.96 miles). Once these obligatory rituals of the umrah (which take a few hours) have been completed, men shave their heads, while women cut an inch or two of their hair to exit the state of being a pilgrim.

For Eliade, the sacred space marks a break from the locus of mundane, profane life. It is an anchor emerging through divine revelation, from which believers orient themselves, allowing access to a more primordial state of being. In the state of ihraam – eyes upon the anchor that had shaped my worship – my experience was more metaphysical than embodied. In those moments, I occupied an imagined Mecca, the fabled city of prophets and angels, and of mothers striving to keep faith in the face of cruel oppression. I could almost see what had been here before, the ghosts of a nascent faith, taking its first shaky breaths, keeping step with the flesh-and-bone believers centuries away.

Accessing that spiritual world required me to suspend my disbelief – because, in 2026, even the Great Mosque is, like Mecca itself, very different from the one I had read about in prophetic traditions. In the past decade, the mosque has been subject to a massive expansion and renovation project. At a cost of nearly $26.6 billion, the Saudi government has rebuilt the complex, growing it from 414,000 square metres to 1.564 million square metres of space, in order to accommodate a growing number of pilgrims and to make the area more accessible. However, this has come at a great cost to the historicity of the space and, to an extent, to the otherworldliness that the line between sacred and profane demands.

Except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the complex have been either modified or destroyed

Four floors of marble walkways now surround the Kaaba, allowing more people to circumambulate at once. The different floors are accessed through a network of escalators and ramps. The final walkway comes with tracks for golf carts – and, at the price of 300 Saudi riyals ($80), pilgrims can complete their rituals on wheels. Those on a budget, meanwhile, can spend half that amount to rent a wheelchair if they’re struggling with walking more than the 2.5 miles expected.

In her travelogue Pilgrimage to Mecca (1934), Lady Evelyn Cobbold, the first British female convert to make the Hajj, wrote:

Even the Ford Motor could not vulgarise the lovely moon-splashed desert, whose stillness was unbroken by a camel caravan we passed, silently treading its way Northward; mysterious phantoms of beasts and men of another world than ours – I inwardly prayed that the motor may never displace the camel.

I wonder what she would make of the carts zipping through the mosque itself today. The consequence of these efficiency-oriented measures is that, except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the Mecca complex have been either modified or destroyed.

The path between the hills of Safa and Marwa, where Muslims believe that the Prophet’s wife Hagar foraged for water, before the spring of holy water, Zamzam, miraculously burst open, has now been flattened and reconstructed as a multistorey, air-conditioned enclosure. The structure that marked the well of holy water has also been demolished, with pilgrims now able to access the water only through taps and tanks. Canopies dedicated to influential classical scholars of Islam within the mosque complex have been dismantled, while neon lights have been installed to mark the point at which circumambulation is to begin.

As I went through the rituals, the chasm between the sacred space in my mind and the very real, remade-for-modern-convenience one I occupied provoked a kind of grief. I mourned that these weren’t the same floors the forebears of my faith had walked, nor were these the pillars they had leaned against. On one hand, that sense of communitas with the other pilgrims nourished my soul; on the other, I was palpably aware of how much of a disjuncture I was at with the past. When I completed my pilgrimage, I reached under the swathes of my hijab to snip off a few curls from my head with small metal scissors. Exiting the state of ihram and physically changed by my acts of worship, I was pushed into a painful awareness of the mundane, profane world. The disjuncture became significantly more pronounced when I stepped out of the mosque.

In Cobbold’s memoir, written less than a century ago, Mecca is the city without walls, protected by mountains, with Bedouin caravans selling wares to pilgrims staying in modest homestays and camping on the desert trail. That Mecca no longer exists either. The homestays are gone, and the hospitable locals of yore now live on the outskirts of the city – their neighbourhoods swallowed up by hotels and shopping complexes.

Some changes are unavoidable. When Muhammad performed his final pilgrimage in 632 CE, an estimated 30,000 followers accompanied him. When I performed my pilgrimage in February 2026, an estimated 1.68 million people from abroad had been granted pilgrimage permits for the month of Ramadan. These pilgrims need space not just to worship, but also to sleep and eat, and to do all that mortal bodies do – and so infrastructure should be built to support those needs.

However, the de-historicisation of Mecca has been a calculated, ideological project, with what would be considered protected monuments in any other part of the world decimated to build vanity projects. Saudi Arabia’s premier religious ideology – Wahhabism – is an 18th-century revivalist movement that espouses a literalist, strict interpretation of the Quran, and it has encouraged the tearing down of historical sites such as the houses of early Islamic figures, and the enshrined gravesites of the Prophet’s family, claiming that they’d invite idolatry otherwise. The refitting of Mecca is also deeply entwined with the rise of the petrodollar in the Kingdom, creating a tense intersection where ritual jostles with capitalism for space. As the writer and public intellectual Ziauddin Sardar puts it in The Sacred City (2014), the Kingdom has made a steel and glass heaven of consumerism in the name of extinguishing idol worship.

Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we battle excess and the temptation of abundance

So, now, a Hilton Hotel stands where the house of Islam’s first Caliph, Abu Bakr, once stood. A nondescript library stands in place of the home in which Muhammad was born, while an 18th-century citadel was torn down to make way for the Makkah Clock Tower complex, a collection of seven buildings that are part mall, part hotel. The tallest of these buildings is a Big Ben-esque structure, sporting a giant clock dial that overlooks the Kaaba.

On the back of the oil economy, the Kingdom has exported its brand of Wahhabi Islam across the world. Traditional ways of believing have been homogenised, and a dogmatic, cookie-cutter version of the faith has been parcelled off. In return, the Global North has exported the phenomenon of placelessness to Saudi Arabia, whereby an influx of foreign brands has remade both the country’s high streets and consumer choices. The commercial onslaught, compounded by the active destruction of material history, gives the fringes of sacred space a particular tone. Irfan al-Alawi, a theologian and heritage preservation proponent, described this in The Guardian as the ‘Manhattanisation of Mecca’.

As I walked through the grey concrete streets and glass malls of Mecca, I wondered if devotion here would have meant more when the skyline was dotted with sandy hills, and there was nothing but the House of God as your harbour against the angry desert. I contemplated whether my return to a comfortable hotel bed, and not a flimsy tent, implied something lacking in my commitment to giving up the material. Or perhaps it is just that I am of this time, and my prayers are subject to its whims. Indeed, perhaps it is in that very unease that ritual finds meaning – if all the world were holy, we would not gravitate as we do to the omphalos (literally, ‘navel’). The sacred is significant because it disrupts the profane. Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we must battle excess and the temptation of abundance.

I can’t presume to know what God thinks of today’s Mecca. After all, to evolve is natural to the holy city; it has been moulded to dynasties and clerical moods over centuries. Belief continues to move past anachronisms, and yet, as one prays by the black-and-gold cloth-covered Kaaba, the shadow of the clock towers falls upon you – a too-obvious metaphor in action.

title: The Secret Lives of Japanese Temple Frogs
content:
Japan is home to tons of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines (which you should be sure to visit if you ever find yourself there). These picturesque locales—numbering in the hundreds in cities like Kyoto—offer serene oases in busy urban environments for both people and wildlife alike. According to a new study published in Urban Ecosystems, frogs in particular are drawn to their many water features, making the landmarks both culturally and ecologically important.

Featured Video

Curious about amphibian life among these watery respites, environmental scientists from Kyoto University set out to catalog their frog populations. The team focused on 31 temples, shrines, and adjacent areas in Kyoto's Higashiyama region, surveying their various ponds and streams for signs of frogs. 

The team took a comprehensive approach, visually identifying frogs, tadpoles, and eggs, collecting samples to analyze environmental DNA, and even recording the various croaks and chirps they heard there. They also collected data on the characteristics of the water features (ponds versus streams, the presence or absence of koi, types of vegetation, and so on).

Read more: “The Wild, Secret Life of New York City”

“We observed amphibians at considerably more waterbodies than we had expected, and this made us realize just how rich in wildlife the local watersides—including those around temples and shrines—truly are,” study author Kae Okoshi said in a statement.

Altogether, they found that Kyoto’s shrines and temples were home to at least seven species of frogs (six native, one invasive). Some of the species they found are, at the bare minimum, regionally threatened, including Bufo japonicus, the Japanese common toad. Additionally, a tree frog species (Zhangixalus arboreus) and the lone fire-bellied newt species they discovered (Cynops pyrrhogaster) are listed as “​​requiring attention” in the area.

According to the team, the differing ornamental land- and waterscaping of the shrines and temples could influence the species of frogs each location attracts. “For example, overhanging trees planted for aesthetic reasons may facilitate foam nesting by Zhangixalus arboreus, whereas canals and spring-fed channels maintained for water management may provide lotic microhabitats suitable for Rana tagoi [Tago’s brown frog],” they wrote. 

Taken together, these characteristics could present a kind of “cultural filter,” the researchers say, screening out some frogs and welcoming others.

It’s an important reminder that while we may engineer wild spaces in urban centers primarily for people, our choices can have unintended consequences that reverberate down the food chain—for better or worse.
